name: English Separatists
notes: The broad movement predates this node’s retained 1606 immediate-Baptist-context marker. Separatism did not universally entail believer’s baptism.
summary: English Protestants who concluded that reform required gathering churches outside the established Church of England.
formation_narrative: Separatists went beyond Puritans who hoped to reform the national church from within. They formed dissenting communities, sometimes fled to the Netherlands, and developed different forms of church order. Smyth and Helwys belong to the part of this story that became Baptist; the wider movement also fed Congregational and Plymouth traditions. The existing 1606 date marks the immediate early-seventeenth-century Baptist context, not the beginning of all English Separatism.
core_beliefs: Voluntary fellowship: churches should consist of committed Christians rather than everyone in a territorial parish.
Reform by Scripture: worship, ministry, and discipline should be tested against the biblical pattern rather than accepted solely because the established church authorized them.
Diversity before Baptist identity: separation from a state church did not itself mean rejection of infant baptism. Baptist convictions developed in one stream later.

key_figures.name: Robert Browne
key_figures.summary: An early English Separatist advocate whose name became associated with Brownist dissent; later Separatists did not all follow the same theology or church order.

key_figures.role: Separatist minister whose congregation later adopted believer’s baptism
key_figures.summary: An English minister whose search for a scriptural church led him from Anglican and Separatist settings into believer’s baptism and then toward Mennonite fellowship.

key_figures.name: Thomas Helwys
key_figures.role: leader and supporter of the congregation’s exile
key_figures.summary: An English exile leader who helped organize the Amsterdam Baptist community, returned to England, and defended liberty of conscience.

key_documents.title: A True Confession
key_documents.significance: An exile Separatist church’s statement of faith and church order. It represents a particular community, not every Separatist and not a general adoption of believer’s baptism.

profile_scope: No single confession or founding assembly governed this diverse movement. The broad name and the narrow 1606 start date remain a modeling limitation. The 1596 confession now supplies a specific primary-document example; it is not a movement-wide standard. No formal corporate dissolution is asserted for this historical process. The status is unknown at the institutional level; the ending narrative explains its diffusion or development.
ending_narrative: Separatism did not end in a universal dissolution. Exile congregations and English dissenting churches developed into several traditions, including Congregational and Baptist forms. The Amsterdam congregation is one documented development, not the only successor to all Separatists; no exclusive institutional successor is assigned here.

name: Early Baptist congregation (Amsterdam)
notes: First Baptist church formed in Amsterdam in 1609.
summary: The English exile congregation associated with John Smyth and Thomas Helwys, conventionally identified as an early Baptist church.
formation_narrative: After leaving England for Amsterdam, Smyth’s congregation reconsidered whether infant baptism could constitute a church of professing believers. Around 1609 Smyth baptized himself and fellow members. Contact with Waterlander Mennonites then raised questions about that act and about the nature of a true church. Smyth sought Mennonite fellowship; Helwys opposed that course and eventually returned to England. The congregation’s importance lies in this contested process rather than a fully settled later Baptist system.
core_beliefs: Professed faith before baptism: church membership was reconstructed around people able to confess faith and repentance themselves.
Biblical church order: the congregation sought to recover New Testament practice even when that meant revising its earlier Separatist position.
Unsettled theology: the precise timing of Smyth’s move away from Calvinism remains debated; describing the congregation as uniformly General Baptist from its first day oversimplifies the evidence.

key_documents.significance: Helwys’s church’s declaration after the dispute with Smyth. It distinguishes that party’s developing position from both earlier Separatism and Mennonite affiliation.

profile_scope: The year is conventionally 1609; Holmes’s study explicitly qualifies the dating and disputes a simple early Arminian narrative.
ending_narrative: The exile congregation divided as Smyth sought Mennonite fellowship and Helwys rejected that course and returned to England around 1612. It therefore ceased to be a single united starting community. The Baptist movement node links to one continuing historical trajectory, while the Mennonite connection is outside the present graph.

name: Eastern Orthodox tradition
notes: Eastern tradition centered in Constantinople and the Eastern churches after the East-West Schism.
size_estimate: more than 200 million adherents worldwide (early 21st century)
summary: A communion of self-governing Eastern churches united by shared faith, sacramental life, and episcopal tradition.
formation_narrative: Eastern Orthodox churches developed within the ancient Christian world through councils, liturgy, monastic life, and regional episcopal structures. Growing estrangement from the Latin West culminated in a separation conventionally marked by 1054 and deepened by later conflict. That date is not the beginning of Eastern Christianity. No single modern founder created the tradition, and self-governing churches do not relate to one another as branches of a single national denomination.
core_beliefs: Trinitarian and Christological faith: ecumenical creeds and councils guide teaching about God and Christ.
Holy Tradition: Scripture is read within the worship, teaching, and historical life of the church rather than separated from it.
Sacramental communion: liturgical worship and the life of prayer express participation in Christ; conciliar relationships distinguish this structure from centralized papal government.

key_figures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
key_figures.summary: A fourth-century Alexandrian bishop and theologian who defended the Nicene account of Christ. He belongs to the tradition’s ancient formation, not to a supposed founding of Orthodoxy in 1054.

key_dates.label: Sack of Constantinople deepens the rupture

key_documents.title: Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
key_documents.significance: Foundational confession used in Orthodox worship; dates refer to the council tradition, not the birth of an Orthodox denomination.

profile_scope: No single founder applies. The model’s 1054 start and Baptist-Europe storage location remain abstractions requiring explicit explanation.
ending_narrative: Eastern Orthodox churches continue as a communion of self-governing bodies. The deepening rupture with Rome was not the dissolution of the Eastern churches, and no single terminal successor can represent the whole tradition.
